posts.caption:
Most apparel brands shoot 40 SKUs when the collection has 70. The budget runs out, and the rest go live with whatever photo exists.

We started GenWear to remove that ceiling.

It's an AI product photography studio for apparel brands. You send a product photo; we send back a campaign — on-model, ghost mannequin, multiple backdrops, cropped for your PDP and your ad sets. No model booking, no studio hold, no shoot date your whole drop calendar quietly depends on.

This account is going to be mostly proof. Crops you can zoom into, the garments we get right, and the ones we still don't.

Which SKU in your catalogue has the worst photos right now?

— GenWear

Every AI photo tool looks perfect at thumbnail size. Zoom to 200% and most of them fall apart.

So here's the crop nobody asks for: the placket of a generated gingham shirt, blown up until you can count threads.

Warp and weft visible in the weave. Stitch tension around the buttonhole. The mother-of-pearl button catching light the way a real one does. Nothing smeared into mush where the detail got difficult.

That's the standard we hold. If a garment doesn't survive this crop, it doesn't go on your product page — and we'd rather tell you that before you pay than after.

Pinch and zoom. Tell us what you find.

— GenWear

The fastest way to judge an AI photoshoot is to hand it your worst SKU.

Sign up, spend the free credits, and a five-pose set comes back in about five minutes — front, back, profile, three-quarter — from one product photo already sitting in your Drive.

Prefer we handle it? Courier the garment instead and the full set comes back within a day. Real fabric gives us better drape and weave reference, so the difficult pieces come out stronger that way.

Don't start with your easiest product. Start with the busy print, the sequinned piece, the white-on-white that never photographed right.

Which one is it? Tell us in the comments or DM the SKU.

— GenWear

Occasionwear is the hardest category to photograph and the one that can least afford a shoot day.

One lehenga. It has to reach a buyer in Surat, an exhibition in Delhi and your website in the same week — so it is almost never lying still in a studio when you need the images.

That is what GenWear is for. One product shot goes in — hanger or mannequin, exactly as you already photograph it. What comes back is a campaign: the same piece on different faces, different ages, different markets, without booking a single model.

Slide 5 is the one that matters. Metallic thread is where AI usually falls apart — zari turns to mush, sequins smear, dabka loses its direction. Zoom in on the thread twist and the bead placement. That is the whole test.

Ethnic and occasionwear brands: send us your hardest piece. The one with the heaviest work, the one you assume no AI can handle. That is the one we want.

— GenWear

posts.slot: CAROUSEL — you can do this yourself
posts.caption:
You do not need us to make an AI model shot. You need us to make the same one twice.

Here is the test, run in the open. One prompt describing a sage green block-print kurta. Four runs, back to back, nothing edited, nothing cherry-picked.

Four different kurtas came back. The motif changed. A hem border appeared and then vanished. The placket moved. New model, new room, new light every time.

Every one of them is a nice photograph. Not one of them is a product you can sell, because your customer is buying one specific kurta — the one in your warehouse, with your print, your buttons, your hem. A catalogue cannot be built out of four near-misses, and re-prompting does not fix it. The tool has nothing to anchor to.

Slide 6 is the same prompt with an anchor: one reference image, then poses generated against it. Same leaf motif, same spacing, same gold placket, every frame. That is the entire difference, and it is the thing GenWear is actually built to do — except the anchor is your product photo, not something we invented.

Two things we are being upfront about: these ran on Gemini 3 Pro Image, and the reference in slide 6 was itself generated rather than shot. We have not run the same four-run test on ChatGPT or Midjourney.

If you have — post what you got. We would like to see it.

— GenWear

We picked the print our own team was most nervous about.

Dense small-scale botanical repeat. Three colours. The kind of pattern that turns into mush the second a model moves — or the second an AI tool tries to reproduce it.

GenWear held it. Weave visible. Print registration intact. Seam-to-seam continuity where the sleeve meets the body.

Here's the standard we hold ourselves to: if the garment survives a 200% crop, it's good enough for your product page. If it doesn't, we don't ship it.

Zoom all the way in. That's the whole pitch.

— GenWear

You upload one product photo. That's the entire brief.

No model booking. No studio hold. No three-week wait for a shoot date that slips because a SKU arrived late from the vendor.

Front, back, profile, three-quarter — five poses in five minutes, on your own login. Prefer to send us the physical piece? Courier it and we'll deliver the full set within a day; fabric behaviour reads better off the real thing.

The kurta in this video started as a flat lay on a table. Everything after that is GenWear.

— GenWear

Everyone told us occasionwear would break it.

Fair. Zari is the hardest surface in Indian apparel — metallic thread that changes colour with the light, sequins that throw specular highlights, dabka work with actual physical depth. Get it slightly wrong and it reads as printed-on rather than stitched-on.

So we ran a hand-embroidered emerald lehenga through it. Every bead sits where the karigar put it. The gold behaves like metal, not like a gold-coloured JPEG.

If you sell lehengas, shararas, or anything with hand-work, this is the test that matters. Ask any vendor to show you this crop before you sign.

— GenWear

Monday it was a studio shirt. Thursday it's a Bandra shirt.

Same SKU. Same print. Different sun, different wall, different energy entirely.

Here's the thing nobody says out loud: your catalogue isn't limited by your creative direction. It's limited by the one location your budget could cover on shoot day. Everything after that is compromise dressed up as a decision.

GenWear removes the location line from the budget. Studio, street, rooftop, Jaipur haveli — pick the backdrop the garment actually deserves.

— GenWear

One shirt. Six completely different campaigns.

Most brands shoot a garment once, get one mood, and live with it for the whole season. Not because they want to — because a second shoot means a second budget.

GenWear takes the same physical piece and re-lights it, re-casts it, re-locates it. Minimal luxe for the website. Street for Reels. Festive for the October push. Same garment, same fit, same fabric behaviour.

You're not choosing a look anymore. You're choosing all of them.

— GenWear

Let's do the actual arithmetic.

A mid-tier catalogue shoot in Mumbai:
Model — ₹60,000
Photographer + assist — ₹40,000
Studio — ₹25,000
HMU + styling — ₹20,000
Post-production — ₹30,000

₹1.8L, and three weeks from brief to approved assets. Then one SKU arrives late and the whole schedule slides.

The kurta at the end took five minutes.

We're not the cheap option. We're the option where your drop calendar stops depending on a shoot date.

— GenWear

Nobody selling AI photography posts the failures. We're going to.

Three places GenWear still isn't good enough:

1. Heavy sheer layering. Organza over organza, where you can see two prints through each other. We get close. Close isn't shippable.

2. Tiny logo text. A woven label under 6mm reads as a smudge. We composite the real label back in rather than pretend.

3. Hands actively gripping fabric. Fingers plus drape plus tension is the hardest problem in the category, and anyone claiming they've solved it is showing you their best frame out of forty.

We flag these before you sign, not after you've paid. That's the difference between a vendor and a tool.

— GenWear

The most common question in our DMs: what do you actually need from us?

A product photo. That's it — the flat lay or hanger shot already sitting in your Drive is enough to start.

Sign up, use the free credits, and a five-pose set comes back in about five minutes. On-model, ghost mannequin, multiple backdrops, sized for your PDP and your ad sets.

If you'd rather we handle it, courier the physical garment instead. Real fabric gives us better drape and weave reference, and we deliver the finished set within a day.

Photos are enough. The garment is better. Both work.

— GenWear

Menswear. Womenswear. Ethnic. Athleisure. Kidswear.

Most brands run three or four different photographers across categories, because the person who shoots your lehengas is rarely the person who shoots your joggers. Then the catalogue looks like four brands stapled together.

One pipeline across the whole range means one light, one grade, one standard. Your feed finally reads as a single brand instead of a collection of shoot days.

What's the category you've never been happy with the photos for? Tell us in the comments.

— GenWear

₹1.8L and three weeks, or five minutes.

We keep coming back to this because it's the only number that changes a founder's mind.

It isn't really about the money. It's about what the money forces you into: shooting 40 SKUs when the collection has 70, because that's where the budget ran out. Reusing last season's images for the pieces that didn't make the cut. Launching a drop with three products that have no model shots at all.

Those 30 unshot SKUs are the actual cost of a studio day. Not the invoice.

— GenWear

Open call, and we'd rather you make it difficult.

Pick the one SKU your last shoot handled worst. The busy print. The sequinned piece. The white-on-white that never photographed right. The one you quietly stopped pushing because the images didn't do it justice.

Send us that one. Free credits, five poses, roughly five minutes.

Then zoom in as far as your screen goes and judge us on the crop, not the pitch.

DM us the SKU, or drop a comment and we'll come to you.

— GenWear
